name: Bonnor-Faulkes Oscillating Sphere
description: A ball of perfect fluid of uniform density whose pressure vanishes at its surface, joined to Schwarzschild's vacuum outside, that can collapse, turn round, or oscillate for ever. Held still it is Schwarzschild's interior; with the pressure gone it is a ball of falling dust.
convention: We keep factors of $c$ and $G$ explicit, and $m = GM/c^2$ is the mass of the sphere as a length. The Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.
history: Uniform density is the simplest thing a star can have, and Karl Schwarzschild had a static star of that kind by 1916 [thompson1967]. Its pressure is greatest at the centre and falls to zero at the surface, where Schwarzschild's vacuum takes over [bonnor1967oscillating]. J. Robert Oppenheimer and Hartland Snyder set the same ball moving in 1939, after taking its pressure away, so that their dust fell freely to a point [thompson1967]. What happens in between? A ball whose density stays the same throughout as it moves, while its pressure still pushes outward, can fall in, turn round, or swing in and out for ever [bonnor1967oscillating].¶I. H. Thompson and G. J. Whitrow, at Imperial College in London, took up the moving ball first, and sent in their analysis in August 1966 [thompson1967]. They followed spheres that contract all the time, with the density uniform at each instant and a pressure gradient inside [thompson1967]. Every such sphere crushes itself to a point of infinite density in a finite time on a clock riding with the fluid, as the dust does [thompson1967]. To an observer outside, the surface only creeps closer and closer to its gravitational radius [thompson1967]. Thompson and Whitrow thought it possible that "in some cases the radius of the model may oscillate" [thompson1967].¶W. B. Bonnor and M. C. Faulkes, at Queen Elizabeth College in London, went after a sphere that moves for ever and never becomes singular, and their reasoning was blunt: "If general relativity is a good physical theory, such solutions must exist" [bonnor1967oscillating]. They wrote the inside in comoving coordinates in which space at each instant is flat space scaled by a factor that varies from the centre to the surface [bonnor1967oscillating]. One function of time, $F$, drives the motion, while a number $\alpha$ and a length $L$ set its shape [bonnor1967oscillating]. The density is the same everywhere at each moment and the pressure falls to zero at the surface $r = r_0$, so the ball joins Schwarzschild's vacuum outside at a moving boundary [bonnor1967oscillating]. With $F = 1$ and two relations among the constants, the ball stands still and is Schwarzschild's static star in isotropic coordinates [bonnor1967oscillating].¶The function $F$ moves like a particle in a potential well, with $\dot{F}^2$ for its kinetic energy, and constants chosen a little away from the static star's open a well with room to rock [bonnor1967oscillating]. With $\alpha = 0.7$, $r_0^2/L^2 = 4/9$, and $m = 0.1084L$, the sphere swings between $F = 0.84$ and $F = 1.20$ with a period of $17.4L/c$, its density and pressure positive throughout [bonnor1967oscillating]. Bonnor and Faulkes had quasars in mind. At a mean density of $10^{-8}$ grams per cubic centimetre the same sphere has $r_0 = 2.8 \times 10^{17}$ centimetres and a mass of $6.1 \times 10^{44}$ grams, and repeats every 7.6 years [bonnor1967oscillating]. They offered it as "the oscillations of a very dense and massive quasar", provided the energy the quasar pours out could be neglected [bonnor1967oscillating].¶With exactly the static star's constants, $\dot{F}^2$ is negative on either side of $F = 1$, so the static star cannot swing in this way [bonnor1967oscillating]. Moved by amounts as small as you like, the constants give small oscillations of period $2\pi\sqrt{6}L/c\sqrt{(1 - \alpha)(1 + 2\alpha)}$, and the static star is stable to them whenever $0 < 2m/r_0 < 16/27$ [bonnor1967oscillating]. Bonnor and Faulkes found this in keeping with the instability Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar had found in 1964 for a star whose surface lies inside $9m/4$ [bonnor1967oscillating]. Other constants, $\alpha = 1$, $r_0^2/L^2 = 2$, and $m = \sqrt{2}L/2$, give a sphere that bursts out of zero volume, reaches a largest radius, and falls back to zero volume in a finite time [bonnor1967oscillating]. Send $L$ to infinity and the pressure vanishes everywhere, leaving a ball of dust whose inside is a flat Friedmann universe [bonnor1967oscillating].¶Every member of the family is conformally flat, so its Weyl tensor vanishes and all of its curvature is the fluid's [sussman2000stephani]. These are the spherically symmetric Stephani universes, perfect fluids whose density depends on time alone while their pressure depends on time and radius [sussman2000stephani]. Roberto A. Sussman, surveying them, listed Bonnor and Faulkes's sphere among their uses as models of stars and cited it for a bounce [sussman2000stephani]. With uniform density and a pressure that varies with radius, the fluid has no equation of state tying its pressure to its density alone [bonnor1967oscillating]. Bonnor and Faulkes were content with that, since their conditions keep the gravitational and the inertial mass density of the fluid from ever turning negative [bonnor1967oscillating].

related.text: Held still, with $F = 1$ and two relations among the constants, the sphere is Schwarzschild's static star of uniform density in isotropic coordinates [bonnor1967oscillating].
The same kind of ball with its pressure taken away, falling freely. Send $L$ to infinity here and the pressure vanishes, leaving dust from a flat Friedmann universe [bonnor1967oscillating].
The vacuum outside the sphere, joined to the fluid at a moving surface where the pressure vanishes [bonnor1967oscillating].
Friedmann's universes are conformally flat too. Among the Stephani universes they are the ones whose fluid falls freely [sussman2000stephani].
